messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had been a painter for thirty years, a man who found his world in color and form. His life with his wife, Ama, had been the steady ground beneath his feet. That ground vanished six months ago on a Tuesday. He was working on a large mural in a new corporate lobby, a swirl of blues and golds, when Ama stopped by with lunch. She was smiling, holding up the bag, when she simply collapsed onto the polished concrete floor. The memory is not a story for Kofi, but a series of searing, silent pictures: the vibrant fabric of her dress against the grey floor, the frantic look in the eyes of a security guard, the piercing blue-and-white flash of the ambulance lights reflecting in the lobby's glass walls. He remembers no sound, only the overwhelming feeling of a world ending.

In the weeks that followed, these images became his unwelcome companions. He tried to return to the mural, believing that finishing it would be an act of honor. But stepping into the lobby, his workplace, was like stepping back into the moment of impact. The sight of the spot where she fell would instantly conjure the fragmented visual memories, and with them, an annihilating wave of grief. The distant wail of a siren on the street outside would cause his entire body to seize up, his muscles clenching in anticipation of a danger that had already struck. He had come to believe his life was utterly destroyed by that moment, and being in the place where it happened only cemented that conviction. He abandoned the commission, leaving the mural half-finished, and hasn't picked up a brush since.

This sense of a ruined life began to poison everything. The belief that he was no longer the man he once was—that vibrant, creative person was gone, replaced by this hollowed-out shell—left him feeling profoundly isolated from everyone, even his own family. This conviction of his own ruin made him exquisitely sensitive to any reminder of his loss; a conversation about someone's aging parent or a friend's illness would feel like a direct threat, a confirmation that the world was nothing but a series of tragedies waiting to happen. Because he felt so broken and apart from others, he could find no safety anywhere. Even in the familiar quiet of his own home, his body remained on high alert, coiled and tense as if awaiting another ambush. The nights are the worst, when the darkness seems to amplify every creak of the house, and he lies awake for hours, vigilant and certain that something terrible is about to happen.

The different facets of his suffering now feed one another in a relentless cycle. His constant physical tension seems to scan the world for threats, making him hyper-aware of triggers like ambulances or talk of loss, which in turn brings the memories flooding back. The more his body braces for another catastrophe, the more his mind seems to dredge up the images of the last one. Likewise, the memories themselves confirm his deepest fears: seeing Ama on the floor again proves that his life is indeed destroyed and that he is right to feel constantly on guard. Sometimes, the feeling comes without a clear picture—a sudden, crushing weight of grief and terror that descends for no reason, leaving him breathless. This disembodied emotion is almost worse than the images; it reinforces his fear that he is losing his mind, that he has been fundamentally and permanently broken by what happened.

Kofi’s world has shrunk to the four walls of his house. He avoids friends, knowing he cannot bear to hear them talk about their lives, their partners, their futures. The isolation he feels has become a physical reality he enforces himself. He came to therapy at the urging of his sister-in-law, who told him, "Ama would not want you to disappear." Kofi isn't sure who he is anymore, or if the man he was can ever be found again. He is terrified of talking about that day, certain it will shatter what little is left of him, but a small, desperate part of him hopes to one day be able to stand in front of a canvas and feel something other than fear.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe a causal link where the patient's negative beliefs about himself or the world lead to the re-experiencing of the trauma memory.
The vignette does not describe a causal link where the trauma memory increases the patient's sensitivity to triggers or reminders.
